## 5. Core object model

### 5.1 Shapes

A 2-D outline and a 3-D solid are the same *kind of thing* seen in two dimensions: both are
built, combined, moved and measured identically. They are therefore specified as **one contract
with two dimensional specialisations**, not as two parallel contracts that happen to look alike.

```
                    Shape                     the universal contract
              backend tag · | & -             (§5.1, C-15)
        translate/rotate/scale/mirror
              bounds() · show()
                 ╱          ╲
             Flat            Solid            the dimensional specialisations
      linear_extrude         projection  →  Flat
      rotate_extrude         attachment, half-cuts,
      offset  →  Solid       masks (CSG backend)
```

* **C-15 One contract, two specialisations.** `Shape` declares everything true of every shape on
  every backend: the `backend` tag, the boolean
  operators, the transforms, `bounds()`, and `show()` (§6.16). `Flat` and `Solid` extend it and add
  **only** what is genuinely dimensional. A member that both would declare identically MUST live on
  `Shape` instead — that duplication is how `Flat` came to be missing `bounds()` (S-2) and to be
  typed `Any` long after `Solid` was not.
* **C-16 Operations preserve the kind.** Every operation on a shape returns *the same kind of
  shape*, and an operand of a boolean MUST be
  the same kind: `flat | flat` and `solid | solid` are the only spellings, and `flat | solid` is a
  static error, not a runtime surprise. This is C-4 enforced by the contract rather than by
  convention.
* **C-17 Crossing dimensions is explicit and named.** `Flat` → `Solid` happens only through an
  extrusion or sweep; `Solid` → `Flat` only through
  `projection`. Each direction is a method a reader can see at the call site; neither happens
  implicitly.
* **C-18 One declaration site, one name each.** All three protocols are declared together in the
  backend-contract layer (L1), so a change to the
  shared surface cannot land on one dimension and miss the other. `Shape`, `Flat` and `Solid` are
  the only names for them — no aliases: a second spelling of a contract is a second thing to keep in
  step, and `Shape2D` was exactly that.
* **C-19 Colour and distribution belong to the shared contract.** Both are operations on "any
  shape", not on solids specifically, so they SHOULD be members of
  `Shape` (S-37, S-31). They are universal now: the SDF backend's solids carry colour as field
  metadata, and its 2-D shapes gained the same shared mixins the solids had (`Colorable`,
  `Anchorable`, `Distributable`). The gap was never a limit of distance fields — colour is metadata,
  distribution is matrices, and anchoring needs only a bounding box, which an SDF carries exactly.
  It was the 2-D shape having inherited none of it.
* **C-20 The contract is the whole object, and it is measured.** Every public operation a shape
  implements MUST be declared on `Shape`, `Flat` or `Solid`. A
  protocol that declares a third of what the object does is not a contract — it is a subset that
  silently locks typed callers out of the rest, and a caller who follows this library's own typing
  advice (PLAN §2) is exactly who it locks out. `def with_boss(base: Solid) -> Solid: return
  base.attach(...)` MUST type-check; attachment, tagging, distribution, the edge treatments, the
  half-cuts and the colour methods are the library's headline composition features and none of them
  may be reachable only by accident of the concrete class. Conformance is **checked, not asserted**:
  a contract test walks the public attributes of every implementation and fails on any name the
  protocols do not declare, with a named, justified allowlist for the deliberate exceptions. Drift
  between the declared surface and the delivered one is the defect this rule exists to prevent — it
  is how `Flat` came to be missing `bounds()` (S-2), and it recurred at scale immediately after C-15
  closed.
* **C-21 One operation, one name.** A shape operation has exactly one public spelling. Synonym pairs
  — `move`/`translate`,
  `rot`/`rotate`, `fwd`/`forward`, `bounding_box`/`bounds`, `nominal_size`/`size` — double the
  surface a reader has to learn and halve the chance two call sites are written the same way, and
  each one is a second thing to keep in step. Where BOSL2's name and Python's differ, keep BOSL2's
  (B2-3) and drop the other. This is deliberately narrower than D-5: two spellings of a *dimension*
  (`radius`/`diameter`) are a convenience the caller chooses between, whereas two spellings of an
  *operation* are the same call twice.
* **C-22 The dimensional split is earned, not historical.** A member present on one of `Flat`/
  `Solid` and absent from the other MUST be genuinely dimensional
  (C-15). `xflip`/`yflip` on `Flat` alone, `spin` on `Flat` alone, `up`/`down` on `Solid` alone are
  the shape of the defect: nothing about two dimensions forbids the first two, and nothing about
  three requires a separate name for the third. A member that both dimensions can honour belongs on
  `Shape`.
* **C-23 A contract member is typed, or it is on a shrinking list.** C-20 requires the contract to
  cover the whole object; this requires the cover to mean something. A
  member declared `(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any)` is present by name and checked not at all — the
  method is found and every argument is accepted, including the wrong ones, which is worse than a
  missing member because it reads as a promise. Where the two backends' concrete signatures
  genuinely differ in a way no checker can reconcile, the protocol MAY declare the caller's view
  with `Any` (PLAN T-6c); that is a bounded list that only shrinks, not a default. What is *not*
  that case, and MUST be written out rather than listed, is a member whose implementations already
  agree — which was 23 of the first 48, the whole distribution and attachment families. Note what
  does **not** justify a loose declaration: an implementation that is itself loose. A CSG-only
  feature refused on the SDF backend by a `(*_args: Any, **_kwargs: Any)` stub (PAR-3) satisfies
  *any* protocol signature, so the contract is free to declare the real one; the loose stub is a
  fact about the refusal, not a constraint on the contract. Reading it as a constraint is what left
  the attachment family unchecked.
* **C-1** Every shape carries a `backend` tag naming the backend that **produced** it. It is a
  property of
  the object, never a reading of the ambient backend at construction time — a CSG shape built inside
  a `use_backend("sdf")` block is still a CSG shape, and must say so. Booleans and transforms return
  a shape on the same backend; mixing raises `CrossBackendError` naming the conversion that fixes
  it. A tag that reports the ambient backend defeats that guard entirely and turns a clear error
  into an internal one.
* **C-2** Operators are the primary spelling: `|` union, `&` intersection, `-` difference.
* **C-3** Shapes are immutable by convention: every operation returns a new shape, so calls chain.
  `attach()` and `tag()` copy rather than mutate; the `attachments` / `tag_name` setters exist for
  those copies to use and are not part of the public contract.
* **C-4** 2-D and 3-D never mix implicitly; a flat shape reaches 3-D only through an explicit
  extrude or
  sweep, and the contract itself enforces it (C-16, C-17).
* **C-5** Shared behaviour (transforms, directional moves, CSG, colour, tags, distribution) lives
  once in
  the common base, not duplicated per dimension.
* **C-6** Forwarding to a native object is limited to an explicit allowlist, and every forwarded
  name MUST
  exist on the wrapped object and be statically declared.

### 5.2 Geometry objects

* **C-7** `Path` is abstract; `Path2D`/`Path3D` are selected by point dimension. Any API taking a
  polyline
  MUST accept a `Path` — and MUST say so in its signature, not merely tolerate one at runtime: a
  caller feeding one function's result to the next is the normal way to use the library, and it must
  type-check ([PLAN T-4](PLAN.md#2-typing)).
* **C-7a** A public parameter that means *an ordered set of points* — a path, outline, profile,
  polygon or
  point list — MUST be typed as `Path2D`, `Path3D` or `Path`, and MUST NOT accept a bare
  `Sequence[Sequence[float]]` or a NumPy array. **The point type is the contract, not a convenience
  wrapper over one.** A bare sequence carries no dimension, no open/closed flag and no winding, so
  each function that takes one has to re-derive all three, and they do not always agree — the same
  list is a 2-D outline to one function and a degenerate 3-D path to the next. Requiring the type
  moves that decision to the one place that can make it once, at construction. A caller with raw
  points writes `Path2D(pts)`, which is where the points get checked.
* **C-7d** Where only one width will do, the check MUST be for the *concrete* type, not for `Path`.
  `Path2D`
  and `Path3D` are siblings, so a guard that asks only "is this a `Path`?" lets a `Path3D` satisfy a
  `Path2D` parameter and reach a formula that reads columns 0 and 1 and drops z — a wrong answer
  rather than a refusal, which is worse than the bare sequence this requirement set out to remove,
  because it is silent. `require_path(..., expect=Path2D)` performs it, and says how to convert.
* **C-7b** The refusal MUST name the wrapper to apply. Raw points are what a newcomer has —
  literals, a CSV,
  another library's output — so `polygon([[0,0],[1,0],[1,1]])` is the natural first attempt, and the
  error it produces is the library's chance to teach the type rather than merely reject the call
  (E-4).
* **C-7c** `PathLike` remains, but is **internal**: it types the normalisation step inside a
  function body,
  never a public parameter. Its docstring said it was "anything an API that wants a polyline
  accepts", which made the permissive form look like the intended contract at every call site that
  imported it.
* **C-8** `Region` is outlines-with-holes; `VNF` is the vertex/face mesh interchange type. Anything
  that can
  produce a mesh SHOULD be able to produce a `VNF`, so it can be inspected and measured with no CAD
  runtime present.
* **C-9** Geometry objects own their operations as methods and return new objects (C-3).

### 5.3 The anchor language

* **C-10** One enum (`Anchor`) covers faces, edges, corners, and axis presets, each member carrying
  its own
  vector. Any "which face/edge/corner" parameter MUST accept it; new APIs MUST NOT invent a parallel
  string or integer vocabulary.
* **C-11** The `constants.py` names (`TOP`, `LEFT`, `CENTER`, …) are aliases kept for BOSL2
  familiarity;
  `Anchor.TOP` is preferred in new code and examples.

### 5.4 Attachment

* **C-12** A solid can carry attached children, positioned by anchor (`attach`, `position`, `align`,
  `reorient`, `orient`), tagged for boolean resolution (`AttachTag.KEEP` / `REMOVE` / `INTERSECT`),
  and resolved with `diff()` / `intersect()` at realize time.
* **C-13** Attachment is a CSG-backend feature; the SDF backend refuses it explicitly (§7.1).

### 5.5 Parts

* **C-14** Every part is a class (P-8) that resolves its inputs into a frozen **spec object**,
  exposes
  derived dimensions as read-only properties, builds geometry lazily under a `shape` **property**
  (`Screw("M6", length=20).shape`, not `.shape()`), and offers `show()`. Callers can therefore
  *measure* a part without building it.
* **C-14a** Note the deliberate difference in what `.shape` means either side of the FFI boundary:
  on a part
  it is the finished `Solid`/`Flat`; on a backend wrapper (`CsgSolid.shape`) it is the raw native
  handle being wrapped. Docstrings MUST say which one they mean.

---

## 6. Subsystems

Every subsystem below is part of the specified system; each MUST honour the principles in §3, the
resolution rules in §8, and the error contract in §9.

### 6.1 Maths, points and vectors

`math`, `vectors`, `points`, `geometry`, `bounds`

* **S-1** Scalar and vector helpers (`slerp`, `modang`, `quant`, `constrain`, `mean`, `EPSILON`)
  mirror
  BOSL2's maths, implemented on Python/NumPy primitives rather than re-derived.
* **S-2** `Point`/`Vector` are the point types; `Bounds2D`/`Bounds3D` are the axis-aligned box
  types. Every
  shape and mesh MUST report its bounds without rendering — this is part of both the `Solid` and the
  `Flat` contract, not just the 3-D one.
* **S-2b One box type, one meaning.** `bounds()` MUST return a `Bounds2D` or a `Bounds3D` —
  everywhere, on every type that has one:
  shapes on either backend, `Path2D`/`Path3D`, `Region`, `VNF`. It MUST NOT return a bare tuple, a
  NumPy array, or any other pair whose halves the caller has to guess at. `lo, hi = thing.bounds()`
  is the obvious reading of the name, and a method that answers a *centre* and a *size* to that read
  is a silent wrong answer, not an API. The box carries both spellings as properties —
  `min_x`…`max_z`, `center`, `size`, `width`/`length` /`height` — so no caller has to do the
  arithmetic and no implementation has to pick a winner. The raw backend pair stays private
  (`_native_bounds()`); the public name means one thing. A second public spelling of the same box on
  the same object (`bounding_box()` beside `bounds()`, `nominal_size` beside `size`) is the drift
  this rule exists to prevent — one concept, one name (C-21).
* **S-2a** A shape's `size` is its **nominal anchor box**, and is not required to equal its bounding
  box.
  `anchor=` is measured against the box the shape is *designed* around — a gear's pitch circle, a
  regular polyhedron's circumsphere, the plate a snap fitting mounts on — so real geometry may sit
  inside it (a polyhedron inside its circumsphere) or stand outside it (gear teeth past the pitch
  circle, a truss clip's hooks past the cell it grips). `bounds()` reports the geometry and MUST
  prefer the native bounding box; it falls back to `size` only where no native box is available. A
  part whose `size` differs from its `bounds()` MUST say at the declaration which box it is naming
  and why. Tests MUST NOT assert that the two agree.
* **S-3** Line/plane/polygon predicates and intersections (`geometry`) operate on `Point`s and
  `Path`s, and
  honour the `SEGMENT`/`RAY`/`LINE` specifiers.

### 6.2 Transforms and rotations

`transforms`, `quaternions`

* **S-4** Affine transforms are 4×4 matrices; the library provides construction
  (`axis_angle_matrix`,
  `rot_from_to`, `rot_about_axis`), inversion, decoding, and application (`apply`, `reorient`).
* **S-5** `Quaternion` is a class with the full rotation algebra (multiply, slerp, to-matrix,
  to-axis,
  rotate-point), and is the preferred spelling for interpolated rotation.
* **S-6** Shapes expose the common transforms as chainable methods — `translate`, `rotate`, `scale`,
  `mirror`, `multmatrix`, and the directional moves `up`/`down`/`left`/`right`/ `forward`/`back`.

### 6.3 Paths and curves

`paths`, `path2d`, `path3d`, `beziers`, `nurbs`, `rounding`, `turtle`

* **S-7** A `Path` is an ordered point list with an open/closed flag, and owns its measurement
  (length,
  perimeter, tangents, normals, curvature, torsion), its sampling (`subdivide_path`,
  `resample_path`, `select`, `cut`, `closest_point`), and its cleanup (`deduplicate`,
  `merge_collinear`).
* **S-8** Corner treatment (`round_corners`, `smooth_path`) MUST support BOSL2's rounding methods
  (circle /
  smooth / chamfer) and size measures (radius / cut / joint / width) as enums.
* **S-9** Bezier curves and patches (`Bezier`, `BezierPatch`) and NURBS curves and patches
  (`NurbsCurve`,
  `NurbsPatch`) are classes that evaluate, subdivide, and convert to `Path`s or `VNF`s, so they
  interoperate with everything else.
* **S-10** Turtle graphics (`turtle2d`, `turtle3d`) build paths from a command list, and their
  output is an
  ordinary `Path`.
* **S-11** A path MUST be able to become geometry: polygon/region fill, extrusion, sweep, or stroke
  (§6.7).
  "Become geometry" means it returns a **shape** — the caller asked for a solid and must get one,
  not a mesh plus an incantation (S-19a).

### 6.4 Regions

`regions`

* **S-12** A `Region` is a set of outlines with holes, supporting boolean union/difference/
  intersection,
  offset, and decomposition back into `Path2D`s.
* **S-13** Region booleans MUST be exact and independent of any CAD runtime.
* **S-14** A `Region` MUST be able to render as a 2-D shape or extrude to a solid, and to carry
  colour
  through that conversion (§6.12).

### 6.5 Meshes and surfaces

`vnf`, `surfaces3d`, `isosurface`

* **S-15** `VNF` (vertices + faces) is the mesh interchange type: constructed from grids
  (`vertex_array`,
  `tri_array`), from fields (`from_field`), from metaballs (`from_metaballs`), or from skinned
  profiles (`from_skin`); combined (`union`, `join`); cut (`halfspace`, `slice`); measured
  (`bounds`, `volume`); and realized (`polyhedron`).
* **S-16** Height fields and function plots (`heightfield`, `cylindrical_heightfield`, `plot3d`,
  `plot_revolution`) produce meshes from data or a callable, with an explicit sampling range.
* **S-17** Implicit surfaces — metaballs (`mb_sphere`, `mb_cuboid`, `mb_torus`, `mb_capsule`,
  `mb_disk`,
  `mb_octahedron`, `mb_connector`), `metaballs2d`, and `contour` — take an isovalue and a bounding
  box, and MUST expose their sampling resolution as an ordinary resolution argument (§8).
* **S-18** Fillets and textured tiles (`fillet`, `interior_fillet`, `textured_tile`) and the `ruler`
  annotation are part of the surface toolkit.

### 6.6 Sweeps, skins and extrusions

`skin`, `miscellaneous`, `shapes3d/extrusions`

* **S-19** The sweep family MUST cover BOSL2's: `path_sweep`, `path_sweep2d`, `linear_sweep`,
  `rotate_sweep`,
  `spiral_sweep`, `offset_sweep`, generic `sweep`, and `skin` across profiles.
* **S-19a A sweep returns a solid.** Every member of the sweep family returns a `Solid`, so its
  result composes with `-`/`|`/`&` and
  the transforms like any other shape. A caller writing `path.path_sweep(profile) - hole` MUST NOT
  have to know that a mesh was the intermediate, and MUST NOT have to append `.polyhedron()` to a
  call that already said "sweep this into a solid". The mesh stays reachable — `.vnf()` on the
  result, for measuring, joining or exporting without a CAD runtime (C-8) — but it is the detail,
  not the return value.
* **S-19b A return type is one type.** No public callable MAY return a union whose arm is selected
  by one of its own boolean parameters.
  `path_sweep(..., transforms=True)` returning a list of matrices instead of geometry is the pattern
  this forbids: it makes the union unavoidable, so every caller of the *ordinary* case pays for the
  flag with a narrowing they cannot skip, and the documented one-liner stops type-checking. A flag
  that changes the return type is a second function — name it (`path_sweep_transforms()`), and let
  each return one thing.
* **S-19c Sweeps agree on winding.** Every mesh the sweep family produces has outward-facing normals
  and therefore positive `volume()`.
  Two members of one family disagreeing on winding is not a stylistic difference: a mesh handed to
  `polyhedron()` inside-out exports fine on its own and then *adds* material where it was meant to
  cut. Whatever guards this for one member guards it for all of them.
* **S-20** Sweeps take their cross-section orientation method, sampling type, and skin
  vertex-matching method
  as enums (`SweepMethod`, `SamplingType`, `SkinMethod`), never as strings.
* **S-21** Offset-sweep end treatments are objects (`os_circle`, `os_smooth`, `os_teardrop`,
  `os_chamfer`,
  `os_flat`, `os_profile`), so a rim treatment is passed as one value rather than several loose
  parameters.
* **S-22** Other extrusions — `extrude_from_to`, `cylindrical_extrude`, `text3d`, `path_text`,
  `chain_hull`,
  `minkowski_difference` — are part of the specified surface.

### 6.7 Strokes and end caps

`_stroke2d`, `_stroke3d`, `caps`

* **S-23** Any path MUST be strokeable: `stroke(width, closed, endcaps, endcap1, endcap2, joints)`
  yields a
  filled outline in 2-D and a solid tube in 3-D, and `dashed_stroke` yields the dashed form. Both
  are also part of the backend contract, so a stroke works on either backend.
* **S-23a One family, one kind of answer.** A stroke is the **area the pen covers**, so in 2-D it is
  a `Region` — outlines-with-holes, which
  is what a dashed stroke needs and what a stroked region already returned — and in 3-D a `Solid`.
  `Path2D.stroke()` returning a `Path2D` described the *boundary* rather than the mark, and left one
  member of a four-member family answering a different kind of thing from the other three
  (`Path2D.dashed_stroke`, `Region.stroke`, `Region.dashed_stroke` all return `Region`;
  `Path3D.stroke` returns `Solid`). The underlying outline stays reachable through the region's
  `paths`.
* **S-24** End caps and joints are described by one type — `CapType` for the named styles (butt,
  round,
  sphere, circle, arrow variants, diamond, dot, tail, custom) and `CapSpec` for a parameterised or
  custom-path cap. A cap MUST be expressible as a single value passed to
  `endcap1=`/`endcap2=`/`joints=`.
* **S-25** Stroke width, cap geometry and joint geometry MUST scale together, and a decorative cap
  MUST trim
  the body so the finished stroke keeps the requested end position.

### 6.8 Masks, profiles and edge treatments

`masking`, `_edges_lang`

* **S-26** 2-D mask profiles (`mask2d_roundover`, `mask2d_chamfer`, `mask2d_cove`, `mask2d_tear`,
  `mask2d_step`, `mask2d_groove`, …) and 3-D masks (`mask3d_roundover`, `mask3d_chamfer`,
  `mask3d_groove`) are first-class shapes, usable on their own or through a solid's
  `edge_mask`/`edge_profile`/`edge_profile_asym`/`corner_profile`/`face_profile`.
* **S-27** Which edges or corners a treatment applies to MUST be expressed in the anchor language
  (C-10),
  including the `edges=`/`except_edges=` selectors and the axis presets.
* **S-26a A mask does not ask for what its parent knows.** A 3-D mask cuts a solid, and the solid
  already knows its own box, so `size=` MUST be optional and
  derived from the parent when the mask is applied through
  `edge_mask`/`edge_profile`/`corner_profile`/`face_profile` (P-3, D-6). `mask3d_roundover(r, size)`
  demanding two positional arguments — one of which is the parent's dimensions — is P-1 inverted on
  the treatment users reach for most.
* **S-26b Masks are applied by name, not by children.** The edge treatments take the *treatment*,
  not a native handle: `solid.round_edges(Anchor.TOP,
  radius=3)` and `solid.chamfer_edges(edges, chamfer=2)` are the spellings a caller should reach
  for, with `edge_mask(edges, mask)` remaining for a custom `Mask3D`. A parameter named `children`
  typed as a raw native object is OpenSCAD's module-with-children vocabulary surviving into a Python
  API, which B2-2 exists to replace, and it leaks an L2 type through an L3 signature (A-1).
* **S-26c Mask parameters follow the same rules as everything else.** A mask names its size measure
  the way the rest of the library does — `radius=`/`diameter=` through
  `pick_radius()` (D-5), not `r`; `width`/`depth`/`length` rather than `x`/`y` — and takes at most
  one required argument (D-2). `mask3d_groove(width, depth, length)` with three required positionals
  is the case D-2 says is never acceptable.
* **~~S-26d A mask profile is a shape.~~** ~~2-D masks return a `Flat`, not a `Path2D`.~~
  **Withdrawn** (§13 rule 5). Implementation showed
  it makes the primary use worse and breaks the layering: a 2-D mask exists to be *swept along an
  edge*, which needs a path, and the `Mask2D` factories are pure L0 — they build a `Path2D` out of
  arithmetic with no CAD runtime in sight, whereas `Path2D.polygon()` crosses the FFI. Returning a
  `Flat` would force every mask construction through a native runtime that A-2 says L0 must not
  need, to spare a `.polygon()` call in the rarer case. A mask profile is data; `.polygon()` is the
  one step to geometry when a caller wants it. S-26's "first-class" stands — it means the profiles
  are named, reusable values rather than inline point lists, which they are.
* **S-28** Rounding and chamfering MUST be available both as constructor parameters (`rounding=`,
  `chamfer=`,
  and their per-end variants) and as masks, and the two MUST agree geometrically.

### 6.9 Partitions and joinery

`partitions`

* **S-29** A solid MUST be splittable for printing: `partition`, `partition_mask`,
  `partition_cut_mask`,
  `partition_path`, and the half-cuts (`half_of`, `left_half`, `top_half`, …).
* **S-30** The cut profile is an enum (`PartitionCutType`: flat, sawtooth, sinewave, comb, finger,
  dovetail,
  hammerhead, jigsaw, square, triangle, halfsine, semicircle), with spread, gap and slop as
  defaulted parameters.

### 6.10 Distribution and copies

`distributors`

* **S-31** Copying is available in two forms that MUST stay in step: methods on a shape
  (`Distributable`:
  `line_copies`, `xcopies`/`ycopies`/`zcopies`, `grid_copies`, `rot_copies` and its axis variants,
  `arc_copies`, `sphere_copies`, `path_copies`, `mirror_copy`, flips) and the matrix-producing form
  (`DistributableMatrix`) for callers that want the transforms themselves.
* **S-32** `xdistribute`/`ydistribute`/`zdistribute` spread a set of shapes along an axis by their
  own sizes;
  `distribute_on_path` places copies along a path with correct orientation.
* **S-33** Distribution MUST work on paths and 2-D shapes as well as solids.

### 6.11 Textures

`texture`

* **S-34** Named textures (`texture("diamonds")`, ribs, bricks, pyramids, hills, rough, …) come from
  one
  registry, and each is either a height field or a VNF tile — the caller does not need to know
  which.
* **S-35** Anything that can be textured MUST accept the texture by name or object plus the same set
  of
  controls: tile size or repeat count, depth, inset, rotation, and per-texture options.

### 6.12 Colour and display modifiers

`color`

* **S-36** `Color` normalises every input form — CSS name, `#rrggbb`, RGB/RGBA sequences in 0–1 or
  0–255 —
  into one RGBA value, and exposes `rgb`, `rgba`, `alpha`, `hex`.
* **S-37** Colour is applied through chainable methods on anything drawable: `color`, `recolor`
  (recursive),
  `color_this` (this shape only), plus `hsl`/`hsv` construction. Opacity travels with the colour.
* **S-38** The preview modifiers `highlight` (`#`) and `ghost` (`%`) are methods on the same
  contract, so a
  debugging aid is a chained call rather than a different API.
* **S-39** `rainbow` / `rainbow_colors` colour a sequence of objects around the hue wheel.
* **S-40** Colour MUST be available on paths and regions as well as solids, and MUST survive the
  conversions
  between them where the target can carry it.

### 6.13 Import, export and interchange

`svg`, `vnf`, `shapes2d/ops`, `shapes3d/base`

* **S-41** SVG import produces ordinary geometry: outlines (`svg_outlines`), a `Region`
  (`region_from_svg`),
  grouped elements (`svg_element_groups`), and colour-carrying rings (`svg_rings_with_colors`) —
  with curve flattening controlled by the ordinary resolution arguments (§8).
* **S-42** Mesh import (`osimport`, 2-D and 3-D) returns a wrapped shape that joins the fluent API,
  not a raw
  native handle.
* **S-43** `polyhedron()` and `VNF.polyhedron()` are the mesh-to-solid boundary; `VNF` is the
  interchange
  type for anything that wants to inspect or measure geometry without a CAD runtime.
* **S-53 There is a way out of the library.** A caller who has built something MUST be able to write
  it to a file: `shape.export(path)` on any
  shape, `VNF.export(path)` on any mesh, with the format taken from the suffix and overridable. This
  section is titled "import, export and interchange" and specified only import; a modelling toolkit
  whose output can be *displayed* but not *saved* is not finished, and "drive the app yourself" is
  not an answer for a library whose L0 promise is that geometry works with no CAD runtime present
  (A-2).
* **S-54 Export is pure where it can be.** Mesh formats that are pure data — STL (binary and ASCII),
  OBJ, OFF, PLY — MUST be written by
  pybosl2 itself from a `VNF`, with no native runtime involved, so exporting works everywhere
  `import pybosl2` does. A solid exports by meshing to a `VNF` first; where a backend can only mesh
  through its runtime, the requirement is that runtime, not a hand-rolled second mesher. Formats
  that are a CAD kernel's own (3MF, AMF, DXF, SVG out) MAY delegate, and MUST raise naming what is
  missing rather than writing a broken file.
* **S-55 Export refuses to write nonsense.** A mesh that is not watertight, or is wound inside-out,
  is a bug the caller wants to hear about
  before a slicer tells them. `export()` validates (`VNF.is_watertight`, positive `volume()`) and
  raises naming the defect, with an explicit `check=False` for the caller who knows their surface is
  open on purpose.

### 6.14 Parts library

`parts/`

* **S-44** Every part is a class per C-14, driven by a catalogue name or nominal size (P-4).
* **S-45** The library MUST cover the BOSL2 parts set: gears (spur, helical, herringbone, rack,
  ring, bevel,
  worm), screws/nuts/holes and threading (ISO, trapezoidal, acme, square, buttress), drive recesses
  (Phillips, hex, Torx, Robertson), ball and linear bearings, hinges and snap connectors, dovetails
  and snap pins, cube truss, modular hose, NEMA steppers, bottle caps, sliders and rails, tripod
  plates, Platonic solids, FDM walls, wiring bundles, hooks.
* **S-46** Parts MUST expose their catalogue as data (spec objects and tables), so a caller can
  query
  dimensions — and the docs can tabulate them — without building geometry.
* **S-46a Parts honour the active backend.** A part builds through the backend-neutral façade (L3),
  not by importing a backend's module
  directly, so `with use_backend("sdf"): Screw(…)` produces an SDF part. Where a part needs an
  operation only one backend can express, it raises `UnsupportedByBackendError` naming that backend
  (B-4) rather than quietly returning a shape from the other one. Parts are not exempt from PAR-1.

### 6.15 Documentation surface

* **S-47** Every subsystem above MUST appear in the generated API reference under a `DocCategory`,
  and every
  geometry-producing callable MUST carry a rendering example (§10).

### 6.16 Display and output

* **S-48 `show()` is how a shape leaves the library.** It hands the shape to the renderer: inside
  the PythonSCAD app it displays in the viewer, and in a
  script it marks the shape as what the run produces. It is the one call in the library with a side
  effect on the session, and the convention every docstring example ends with.
* **S-49 `show()` returns the shape.** It closes a chain without swallowing the value — `part =
  cuboid([20, 20, 10]).up(5).show()` both
  displays and binds. It MUST NOT return `None`.
* **S-50 `show()` is on the shared contract.** Every shape can be shown, 2-D or 3-D, on either
  backend (C-15). Showing an SDF solid meshes its
  field — that is not the implicit conversion B-5 forbids, because rendering *is* meshing and
  nothing meshed is handed back. Showing a 2-D distance field refuses instead, naming the extrusion
  that would make it renderable: a field over the plane has no rendering of its own.
* **S-51 Builders delegate.** A part or any other builder exposes `show()` as a convenience that
  shows its `shape`, so a caller
  never has to reach inside to display something.
* **S-52 `show()` needs a renderer.** With the pip wheel alone it marks the object for output; the
  PythonSCAD **app** is what puts it on
  screen. Documentation examples therefore end in `.show()` and are rendered by the docs build, not
  by the test suite.

---

## 7. Backend model

* **B-1** The active backend is block-scoped and thread-safe, default `"csg"`; `use_backend("sdf")`
  switches
  it for a block, `set_default_backend()` globally.
* **B-2** A backend implements a small contract: hand back the constructor for a named shape, build
  it, do
  n-ary booleans, extrude paths, and stroke a path.
* **B-3** The **façade owns the default** for every argument both backends understand: it declares
  that
  default in its own signature and always forwards it, so an identical call produces identical
  geometry on either backend (PAR-5). A backend keeps its own defaults only for options exclusive to
  it. Arguments a backend has no notion of MUST NOT be forwarded to it — that filtering is by *what
  the backend declares*, not by *what the caller happened to pass*. The filtering applies to
  **façade-owned defaults only**; a value the caller supplied is subject to B-9 instead.
* **B-4** A backend MUST NOT silently approximate a feature it cannot express; it raises
  `UnsupportedByBackendError` with a hint naming the alternative or the backend that does support
  it.
* **B-5** Conversion is one-directional and honest: SDF → CSG is an exact mesh; CSG → SDF is lossy
  and not
  offered implicitly.
* **B-6** Backend-specific extras stay on the backend's own module.
* **B-7** Adding a façade shape requires: the façade constructor, a matching constructor in both
  backends
  (or an explicit refusal), and a row in the backend matrix tests.
* **B-8** What a caller gets when they leave an argument out MUST be inspectable, not silent:
  `effective_defaults(shape)` reports the active backend's real defaults.
* **B-9** The façade exposes the **union** of what the backends can build, not the intersection, and
  a
  caller-supplied argument the active backend cannot honour raises `UnsupportedByBackendError`
  naming the parameter, the backend, and the way forward. Dropping it is forbidden:
  `regular_prism(radius1=8, radius2=4)` must not quietly return a straight prism on a backend with
  no taper. This is B-4 applied to arguments rather than whole features, and it is what lets one
  body of code — the parts library above all — be written once against the façade and fail loudly
  where a backend falls short, instead of being written twice.
  * A parameter that describes *tessellation* (`fn`/`fa`/`fs`, `realign`, `circumscribe`) is not a
    feature gap on a backend that has no facets: those MAY be accepted and ignored, provided
    `effective_defaults()` says so.

### 7.1 Backend parity

The two backends are meant to be **interchangeable for as much of the library as is viable**. The
same source should build on either, and the set of things that only work on one MUST stay as small
as the mathematics allows.

* **PAR-1 Parity is the default expectation.** Anything that can be expressed as a signed-distance
  field MUST be available on the SDF backend,
  with the same name, the same argument names, and the same meaning as its CSG counterpart.
  Divergence needs a reason, not a shrug.
* **PAR-2 New shared features land on both.** A new façade shape, option, or operation MUST be
  implemented on both backends, or MUST be
  accompanied by an explicit refusal (B-4) and an entry in the gap list. "CSG only for now" is a
  tracked decision, never a silent omission.
* **PAR-3 The exclusive lists are minimal and justified.** `CSG_ONLY_FEATURES` and
  `SDF_ONLY_FEATURES` are the single source of truth for what is exclusive,
  and each entry MUST carry the reason it cannot cross over. An exclusive feature is **declared and
  refuses**, not absent: the backend that lacks it implements the method and raises
  `UnsupportedByBackendError` naming the way forward (B-4). Two reasons. C-13 asks the SDF backend
  to refuse attachment *explicitly*, and a method that says why is more explicit than a missing
  name. And since Python 3.12 an `isinstance` check against a runtime-checkable protocol uses static
  lookup, so a member supplied only by a dynamic fallback makes `isinstance(sdf_solid, Solid)` false
  for a perfectly good solid — which is how the contract would come to exclude the very shapes it
  describes. A caller that needs to know *before* calling consults the exclusive list, not the
  shape. Today that is the attachment/anchor system (CSG-only, because anchoring needs a shape's
  face and edge structure, which a distance field does not retain), `projection` and `fill`
  (CSG-only, because a 2-D shadow of a solid and a filled outline are not derivable in closed form
  from a field — both backends *do* build 2-D shapes otherwise), and the implicit-surface
  `round`/`chamfer` methods that survive transforms (SDF-only, because CSG expresses those as
  constructor parameters). An entry that becomes implementable MUST be removed from the list, not
  left as a permanent excuse; the list is re-reviewed whenever either backend gains a capability.
* **PAR-4 Equivalent options, not just equivalent shapes.** Parity is measured per *option*: if the
  CSG cuboid takes `rounding`, `chamfer`, `edges` and
  `except_edges`, the SDF cuboid MUST take the same ones with the same selector semantics. The
  **façade** spelling is identical on both backends; where a backend's own module spells a parameter
  differently, the difference MUST be declared in one central translation table rather than leaking
  into the façade. The only sanctioned backend-specific control is the resolution knob
  (`fn`/`fa`/`fs` vs `res`).
* **PAR-5 Same code, same result.** For any construction both backends support, the two MUST agree
  on placement, orientation,
  anchoring, bounds, and units — differing only in tessellation detail. This holds for calls that
  omit arguments as well as calls that pass them, which is why the façade owns the shared defaults
  (B-3). The backend matrix tests record what each backend supports, and
  `docs/design/sdf-csg-compatibility.md` is the working plan for closing the remainder.
* **PAR-6 Crossing is explicit.** Mixing operands from two backends raises `CrossBackendError`
  naming the conversion (B-5); the
  library MUST NOT convert silently to make a call succeed.

---

## 8. Defaults and resolution

### 8.1 Argument tiers

| Tier | Meaning | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **T1 — Subject** | *what* is being made: size, spec name, path | At most one, positional, MAY still have a default |
| **T2 — Shaping** | changes the form: `rounding`, `chamfer`, `teeth`, `length` | Keyword; defaults to "off" or to the catalogue value |
| **T3 — Placement** | `anchor`, `spin`, `orient`, `center` | Keyword; defaults `CENTER` / `0` / `TOP` |
| **T4 — Resolution** | `fn`, `fa`, `fs`, `res` | Keyword; defaults to "inherit the ambient value" (§8.3) |
| **T5 — Escape hatch** | `convexity`, `eps`, `method`, `style` | Keyword; defaults to what 95 % of callers want |

* **D-1** T3–T5 MUST be keyword-only; T2 SHOULD be.
* **D-2** One required parameter is the target; a second needs a written justification in the
  docstring;
  three is never acceptable. The justified two-argument cases today are `Screw(spec, length)`,
  `prismoid(size1, size2)` and `regular_prism(sides, …)` — each names two independent dimensions
  that no default can invent.
* **D-3** Defaults MUST be immutable.
* **D-4** `None` means "not supplied, decide for me" — never "off". "Off" is `0`, `False`, or an
  explicit
  enum member.
* **D-5** Where a dimension has two conventional spellings (`radius`/`diameter`), the API MUST
  accept both
  and require neither. Giving both spellings of the **same** dimension is an error, not a silent
  preference: it raises `ValueError` naming both parameters and their values. Spellings at different
  levels of specificity are not a conflict — `radius1` legitimately overrides `radius` — and resolve
  most-specific-first: `(radius1, diameter1) > (radius2, diameter2) > (radius, diameter)`. This is a
  deliberate departure from BOSL2's `get_radius()`, which silently prefers the radius (B2-2, E-5).
* **D-6** A derivable parameter MUST default to "not given" and be derived.
* **D-7** A spec argument SHOULD accept the convenient forms — trade name, plain number, or an
  explicit
  mapping — and collapse them immediately into one frozen spec object.
* **D-8** A façade MUST NOT present as optional an argument its backend requires.
* **G-1 A parameter family that travels together is a group.** A parameter family that appears on
  more than three public callables and is always passed as a unit
  MUST be available as a frozen group object, so it can be built once and reused. `Placement(anchor,
  spin, orient)` is the case that motivated this: 50 callables take all three, another 31 take two
  of them, and every one of those restates the same defaults. `CapSpec` (S-24) is the pattern
  already in the library. A group is a *value*, not a namespace: it is frozen, it composes
  (`with_`), and it carries its own defaults. **A group reads in every dimension its members mean
  something in.** A placement is anchor, spin and orient in three dimensions and anchor and spin in
  two — there is no third axis in the plane to turn a face towards — so one placement serves a 2-D
  profile and the solid extruded from it, which is the case worth having.
* **G-6 A group refuses what a dimension cannot honour.** Where a group means less in one dimension
  than another, the members that do not apply MUST be
  refused rather than dropped. A `Placement` carrying a real `orient` passed to a 2-D constructor
  raises, naming the way forward, because silently honouring two of its three members is the wrong
  answer E-5 forbids — the caller asked for an orientation and got a shape without one, with nothing
  said. The *default* `orient` is not a request: `Placement()` and `Placement(anchor=...)` are
  dimension-neutral and pass anywhere, which is what keeps one placement usable across a profile and
  its extrusion (G-1).
* **G-7 A group makes a conflict unrepresentable, not merely checked.** Where a family's members are
  mutually exclusive, the group SHOULD model the exclusion in its shape
  rather than validate it. `rounding` and `chamfer` are one edge treatment, not two independent
  sizes — an edge is rounded or chamfered, never both — and the library checked that in **six**
  places with six different wordings, not one of which said what to do instead. `EdgeTreatment`
  carries one kind and one size, so there is nothing left to disagree; the loose spellings keep the
  check (G-3), and it is now written once (G-5).
* **G-9 Groups are resolved where the arguments already are.** A constructor taking several groups
  SHOULD resolve them in one call, operating on the arguments it
  is about to forward rather than beside them. The loose members are already listed in that dict, so
  resolving in place costs a constructor one wrapper; resolving beside it cost thirteen lines of
  unpacking in every constructor, which is the transcription B-3 exists to reduce rather than add
  to. `cube` and `cuboid` went from 53 lines to 28 on this change alone.
* **G-8 A parameter is a promise, and an unkept one refuses as a library error.** A parameter in a
  public signature says the library honours it. Where this port advertises one it
  does not build, the refusal MUST be a `Bosl2NotImplementedError` — a `Bosl2Error` so `except
  Bosl2Error` catches it (E-1), a `NotImplementedError` so existing callers are unaffected, and
  carrying a hint naming what to do meanwhile (E-2). Four public callables raised a bare
  `NotImplementedError` instead: `cyl(texture=...)`, `cuboid(teardrop=...)`, `CapType.CIRCLE` and
  `VNF.from_field` with a range. The gaps are listed and the list only shrinks. **`texture=` is the
  one that matters:** S-34 and S-35 specify textures as a working subsystem, the registry is built,
  and thirteen public constructors take the five texture parameters — so grouping those five (G-1)
  would be polish on a promise nothing keeps, which is why the `Texturing` group was not built.
* **G-2 A group composes and inherits.** A group SHOULD offer `with_()` to derive a variant without
  mutating the original, and where the
  family has ambient defaults (§8.3) a way to read them. `None` in a member still means "not given,
  decide for me" (D-4), never "off".
* **G-3 The loose spellings survive, and conflicting with the group is an error.** Introducing a
  group MUST NOT withdraw the loose parameters. `cuboid([60, 40, 12],
  anchor=Anchor.BOTTOM)` is the common case and reads better than wrapping one value in a group;
  BOSL2's names are also kept for exactly this reason (B2-3). Supplying a group *and* one of its
  members MUST raise, naming both — the same rule and the same reasoning as a radius given beside
  its own diameter (D-5): the call cannot mean two things at once, and silently preferring one of
  them turns a typo into wrong geometry.
* **G-4 Resolution's public answer is the ambient default, not a group.** `Facets(fn, fa, fs, res)`
  exists, but as **plumbing**: it carries the four values down a call
  chain as one, which is what R-1 asks for and what a forwarding function most often gets wrong. It
  is not the spelling a caller should reach for, because resolution already has a better public
  answer — `use_defaults(fn=64)` sets it for a whole block without threading anything through any
  call (R-4), and a group passed to every call would be strictly worse. Every public callable taking
  `fn`/`fa`/`fs`/`res` SHOULD say so in its `Args:`, so a reader meets the ambient mechanism at the
  parameter rather than having to find `pybosl2.defaults`.
* **G-5 One resolution rule, in one place.** "An explicit value beats the ambient one" (R-5) MUST be
  implemented once. `resolve_facets` and
  `resolve_res` were two implementations of it — one for the CSG facet controls and one for the SDF
  resolution — which is two things to keep in step for no reason. Both now go through
  `Facets.resolved()`.

### 8.2 Curve resolution is universal

* **R-1** Every construction that produces a **circle, arc, rounding, chamfer arc, sphere, cylinder,
  sweep,
  texture tile, flattened SVG curve, sampled field, or any other tessellated curve** MUST accept the
  facet controls — `fn`/`fa`/`fs` on the CSG side, `res` on the SDF side — and MUST **pass them
  through to every sub-construction it builds**. A part that rounds its corners hands its `fn` to
  the rounding; a gear hands it to its tooth arcs; a mask hands it to its profile; a sweep hands it
  to its cross-section. Dropping them part-way down is a defect.
* **R-1a** The trigger is *generating points that approximate a curve*, not *taking a radius*. A
  callable
  that places or measures geometry from a radius — arc/rot/sphere copy distributors, `polar_to_xy`,
  circle-tangent geometry — is outside R-1, because nothing it returns is tessellated. When it is
  genuinely ambiguous, the deciding question is whether a caller could observe a facet count in the
  output.
* **R-2** These controls MUST never be required: omitted, they inherit (§8.3).
* **R-3** A backend that cannot honour a control MUST NOT be handed it.

### 8.3 Ambient defaults

* **R-4** Resolution SHOULD be settable once for a block rather than threaded through every call:
  `use_defaults(fn=64)` (block-scoped, nesting, thread-safe) and `set_defaults(...)` (process-wide).
* **R-5** An explicitly passed value always wins over the ambient one, and there MUST be a way to
  opt out of
  an ambient value rather than only override it: passing `fn=0` means "ignore any ambient `fn`, use
  `fa`/`fs`", matching OpenSCAD's own `$fn=0`. P-6 applies to ambient defaults as much as to
  signature defaults.
* **R-6** Ambient values are resolved at **construction** time, so a shape's smoothness is fixed by
  where it
  was built.
* **R-7** With nothing set anywhere, the renderer's own defaults apply (`$fa=12`, `$fs=2`).

### 8.4 Units and frame

* **D-9** Lengths are millimetres, angles are degrees, the frame is right-handed Z-up. No API takes
  a unit
  argument; `INCH` converts at the call site.
* **D-10** Shapes are centred on the origin, oriented `+Z`, unrotated by default.

---

## 9. Error contract

* **E-1** All library errors derive from one base error type — and that MUST be true of the
  validation
  errors too, which are the overwhelming majority. E-4 requires them to be `ValueError`s and E-1
  requires them to be `Bosl2Error`s; those are only compatible if the type raised is **both**.
  `Bosl2ValueError(Bosl2Error, ValueError)` satisfies each: `except ValueError` keeps working for
  every caller who already wrote it, and `except Bosl2Error` starts working, which today it does
  not. A contract a caller cannot use in an `except` clause is not a contract.
* **E-2** A refusal names the feature, the backend, and the alternative.
* **E-3** Cross-backend mixing names both operands and the conversion that resolves it.
* **E-4** Argument validation raises `ValueError` naming the offending parameter(s) and the accepted
  spellings. A public entry point MUST NOT `assert` on user input.
* **E-5** A call that cannot mean what it says MUST fail loudly rather than build something else.
  Loudly
  means *raising*: printing a warning and returning one operand unchanged (`flat - solid`), or
  returning a degenerate shape with infinite bounds (`regular_ngon()` with no radius), is the silent
  wrong answer this rule forbids. A minimum-argument test that only asserts "does not raise" does
  not establish E-5 — the result has to be a shape someone could use.
* **E-6 A refusal is still an attribute error.** An error raised from `__getattr__` because the
  backend cannot offer that name MUST also be an
  `AttributeError`, so `hasattr()`, `getattr(x, n, default)`, `inspect`, `copy`, `pickle` and every
  REPL completion keep working instead of exploding. `UnsupportedByBackendError` inherits
  `AttributeError` for this reason; the message is unchanged, and code that probes a capability gets
  `False` rather than a traceback. Refusals raised from a *call* are unaffected.
* **E-7 Dimensional mixing raises.** `flat - solid` raises at runtime, naming the extrusion or
  projection that resolves it (C-4, C-16).
  The static error is the first line of defence and the right one, but this library's users drive a
  CAD app and mostly do not run a type checker, so the contract cannot rest on it alone.

---

## 10. Documentation and catalogue

* **DOC-1** Docs are **generated** from the source: module header tags drive the API reference, and
  docstring
  examples drive the rendered figures. An API list is never hand-maintained.
* **DOC-1a Generation MUST NOT destroy what it did not write.** The generator owns the module stubs
  and `index.rst`; everything else is prose it is a guest among.
  A page it does not recognise is *deleted*, and a hand-edit to a generated file is *overwritten* —
  both silently, because neither raises a warning and a build that removes a page still reports
  success. So a hand-written page is registered with the generator, a link to it belongs in the
  generator rather than in its output, and a test — not a convention — is what keeps the register
  honest.
* **DOC-2** Every public module, class, and callable is documented, and every callable that produces
  geometry
  carries an example that renders.
* **DOC-3** The visual parts catalogue renders each featured part through the real PythonSCAD binary
  and
  reports measured metrics — triangles, volume, bounding box, watertightness. Its caches are
  committed, because CI has no CAD binary.
* **DOC-4** Mechanics — docstring style, header tag values, build commands — are specified in
  [PLAN.md
  §5](PLAN.md).
* **DOC-5 The examples are the contract, so they are checked like one.** Every docstring example
  MUST pass `mypy --strict` as ordinary user code, because that is exactly
  what it is: the example is what a caller copies, and an example the project's own type checker
  rejects is a signature defect the docs found first. `path_sweep`'s documented one-liner failing on
  a union return (S-19b) is the case this rule exists to catch — the mechanics are [PLAN
  §5](PLAN.md), and it is a gate (Q-6), not a review habit.
* **DOC-6 There is a front door.** The documentation MUST open with a task-oriented getting-started
  page that carries a reader from
  installation to a finished, exported part — build, round, cut, place, measure, save — before the
  API reference. §3's promise is that a caller who knows what they want to build but nothing about
  the library can build it; a reference indexed by module is not how anyone learns that, and it is
  the first thing a new user sees. The page's examples run under the same gates as every other
  example (DOC-2, DOC-5).

---

## 11. Quality gates

A change is done when all of these hold (mechanics in [PLAN.md §9–§11](PLAN.md)):

* **Q-1** The full test suite passes on **every supported interpreter — 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13** — and
  the
  pure-geometry tests pass with no CAD runtime present. One interpreter is not enough: the versions
  differ in behaviour this library depends on (`isinstance` against a Protocol resolves differently
  before and after 3.12), so a green run on the newest says nothing about the oldest, which is the
  one CI will run anyway. Mechanics in [PLAN L-1, L-1a](PLAN.md#1-language-baseline).
* **Q-2** Strict static type checking passes with zero errors.
* **Q-3** Lint and format are clean.
* **Q-4** Every new public callable has a minimum-argument test — the mechanical enforcement of P-1
  — and a
  validated docstring example. For façade shape constructors this is enforced automatically by the
  contract tests; elsewhere it is a review obligation until the check is generalised (§12.2).
* **Q-5** The contract tests guarding these rules (mutable defaults, façade honesty, stub parity,
  facet
  coverage, backend matrix, protocol/object agreement, export completeness) still pass.
* **Q-7** The **artifact** passes, not only the source tree. A gate builds the wheel, installs it
  into a
  clean virtualenv, imports it, and type-checks a short consumer snippet against it. Q-1…Q-6 all
  read the working copy, so nothing before this asked what a release actually contains — which is
  how `py.typed` came to be missing from every wheel this project has published while `mypy
  --strict` ran clean on every commit. What ships is a separate claim from what builds, and an
  unmeasured claim is a wish (B2-1).
* **Q-6** Every docstring example type-checks under `mypy --strict` (DOC-5), and every example that
  states a
  value in a trailing comment is executed and held to it (PLAN D-P5b). The examples are user code;
  they are held to what the library asks of user code, and to the truth of what they claim.

---

## 12. Conformance status

The conformance history — every requirement that was open and is now closed, with what was wrong
and what fixed it — lives in [CONFORMANCE.md](CONFORMANCE.md). It is append-only, and a row moves
there in the same commit as the code (§13 rule 4).

### 12.2 Open

| # | Requirement | Current state |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **C-14 / O-2** | **8 of the 51 parts build their geometry in `__init__`** (was 45), where C-14 says a part "builds geometry lazily under a `shape` property... callers can therefore *measure* a part without building it". Nothing measured the claim, so it sat in the spec being false — and the *cost* figure written here to replace it was wrong in turn, overstating the number of affected parts by 3x while understating the price by the same. Measuring it properly is what directed the rest of the work: the waste was never spread evenly across the eager parts but concentrated in a handful where `__init__` ran real Python-side path, sweep or grid math — `RingHook` (57 ms), `ThreadHelix` (51 ms), `SpurGear2d` (26 ms) and the three cubetruss parts (~12 ms together) — so asking one of those for a dimension paid for a full build. Converting those six by hand took the total construction cost of **every** remaining eager part to **~7 ms**, and of the four that expose three or more derived dimensions to **~1 ms**. The eight that remain are eager only in the letter: their `__init__` composes *lazy native ops*, so the backend defers the work regardless and a catalogue query is already cheap — which is why the count stops being the interesting number and the measured cost takes over. Held by `tests/test_parts_are_lazy.py`, whose list only shrinks — 8 left, from 45 — and whose `test_spec_eager_count_matches_the_measurement` parses the count out of this row, because the figure that stood here drifted twice before anything checked it. `Slider` was converted by hand, 27 more by a transformation that grew a guard for each way the split can go wrong, and the six costly ones by hand again once the measurement said where to look. **Converting one is not the mechanical move it looks like:** an automated attempt across six files split `__init__` at the resolved-spec assignments and carried the *validation* into the deferred build with the geometry, so a rejected call stopped raising until someone asked for a shape (45 tests caught it, and it was reverted). A part separates **three** things, not two — validate the arguments, resolve the derived dimensions, then build. Three further reasons the rest resist a script: a part may resolve a derived attribute *in the middle of* its geometry; its validation may be indirect — a spec-object constructor that raises, which no scan for a literal `raise` finds; and a trailing `self._x = y` assignment is only spec if `y` is a name the spec section resolved, not a local the geometry computed. A later guard taught the scan to recognise spec-object constructors by name, which promptly **over-reached in the opposite direction**: with the spec object counted as known, `spec._profile().linear_extrude(...)` read only known names and was swallowed as spec — the very geometry being deferred. Reading attributes off a resolved spec is free; a *call* is where geometry gets built, so the only call the scan accepts is constructing the spec itself. Loosening a rule to convert one more part is how a transformation starts converting things it should not — past that point the remaining conversions were cheaper and safer done by hand. Making the parts lazy also surfaced **three** refusal messages naming the wrong reason: `Worm`, `BevelGear` and `WormGear` all claimed to build "2-D geometry" when all three build a VNF — one copy-paste propagated three times, invisible while the refusal fired generically at construction. |
| 2 | **S-46a / PAR-1** | **40 of the 51 parts build on either backend** (T14), measured rather than asserted by `tests/test_parts_backend_coverage.py`. The 11 that refuse all need the same thing — a non-convex mesh, which has no closed-form distance field — so closing this fully would mean approximating one, which B-5 forbids. **The reason is the gap; the count is not effort left to spend.** These figures were previously stated as "38 of 53, 15 refusing": the total double-counted an alias (`manfrotto_rc2_plate` *is* `ManfrottoRC2Plate`) and neither number had been rerun since parts were ported. All 11 refusals were checked individually and every one cites non-convexity, so the *reasoning* was right where the arithmetic was not — which is precisely why B2-1 says a claim nothing measures is a wish. |
| 3 | **SPEC/PLAN maintainability** | **Closed by T26, T27 and T38.** SPEC.md and PLAN.md are generated from `spec/requirements.toml` and a prose frame, so a requirement has one home; §12.1's history is in [CONFORMANCE.md](CONFORMANCE.md) and T0–T25 in `docs/tasks-archive.md`. **All 275 requirements are triaged** (T38), which is the number the registry was built to produce: **208 enforced** by a named test that fails when the rule is broken, **47 reviewed** — judgements no test can make, each saying why — and **19 unenforced**, each carrying a note describing the guard that is missing. The remaining duplication is the eight rules stated twice (C-7a↔T-4, S-19b↔T-6d, E-1↔E-P4a, C-14↔O-2, S-46a↔O-0a, A-6↔M-2a, R-1↔R-P2, D-5↔E-P5): the registry makes them visible and does not merge them. The five colliding prefixes stay recorded rather than renumbered, ids being permanent (§13 rule 5). |
| 3a | **19 requirements nothing checks** | The triage's real output. Each is mechanically checkable and simply unchecked, and each says in its `note` what the missing guard would do. Three groups. **Signatures nobody scans:** keyword-only-ness (P-5, D-1, T-9a — one signature scan closes all three), required-argument counts beyond the masks (D-2), the facet parameters' spelling (R-P1), anchors typed as strings (O-6b — this is how `text()` kept a `str` anchor until T36), frozen spec objects (O-5), and dynamic-global registration (T-9). **Rules with no ratchet:** `TODO` comments and stubbed bodies (S-3), `typing.Union`/`Optional` (L-2 — ruff's UP rules would do it), the runtime dependency list against pyproject (L-4 — it has already grown twice), the native passthrough allowlist naming real attributes (C-6), and flag-selected return unions (T-6d — PLAN X-4 names a guard for it that does not exist). **Coverage gaps:** `text3d` is the one extrusion S-22 names that nothing tests, textures reach only the cylinder family (S-35), parity is measured per shape and not per option (PAR-4), and `Bounds` is not asserted on every type that S-2 says has one. |
| 4 | **A-1 / A-6 / PAR-1** | **The layering rules are stated and unmeasured, and both have drifted.** 16 L0 modules import L2, four of them at module level (`regions` → `shapes3d`, `path2d`/`path3d` → `miscellaneous`, `turtle2d` → `shapes2d`); the other 12 are function-local, which PLAN M-5 sanctions for a genuine cycle and which is systematic here rather than exceptional. The cause is structural: S-11 requires an L0 path to *become geometry*, and the bridge it uses reaches a backend module directly. So `Path2D.polygon()` (`path2d.py:1465`) imports `pythonscad` itself and is typed `-> Bosl2Shape2D` — inside `use_backend("sdf")` it returns a CSG shape, which is exactly what A-6 exists to prevent and now a PAR-1 defect too, since the SDF backend is a full-parity target. **A-10** (new): an L0 geometry bridge returns `Flat`/`Solid` and builds through the L3 façade. The allowed import edges become data (`spec/layers.toml`) with a test. T29. |
| 5 | **Q-7** (new) | **Nothing tests what is shipped.** Q-1…Q-6 all read the source tree; no gate builds the wheel, installs it, or imports it, so the first person to find out what a release contains is whoever installed it. What that gate found on its first run: the five `.pyi` stubs do reach the wheel — setuptools includes them unasked — and `py.typed` did not, because setuptools does not include *that* unasked. **The marker's absence turned out to cost less than it looks:** measured against mypy 1.20, mypy 2.3 and pyright at default settings, a consumer in a clean virtualenv gets full type information from this package with or without it, each of those checkers reading a library's inline types whether or not it declares them — a wrong attribute name in the consumer snippet is caught either way. So the marker is hygiene, not a defect: PEP 561 is how a library *declares* its types are intentional rather than leaving it to each checker's default. The gate is what matters, and it is the general form of the lesson this file keeps recording — the artifact was never measured, so what it contained was whatever setuptools happened to do. |
| 6 | **C-21 / PLAN S-2** | **Closed by T32.** C-21 was enforced on the shape surface and nowhere else, so `Path2D` and `Path3D` each kept three synonym pairs — `deduplicate`/`deduplicated`, `subdivide`/`subdivide_path`, `resample`/`resample_path`. BOSL2's spelling survived in each (B2-3), `refine=` moved onto `subdivide_path` where BOSL2 has it, and the fuller docstrings moved with the survivors rather than dying with the spellings that carried them. The check now walks every public class reachable from the top level. PLAN S-2 (functions under 50 lines) had **243 violations, the longest at 237**; retiring the rule was the alternative and was rejected, because the rule is right and the code had simply never been held to it. It is a per-file budget that only shrinks — per file rather than one total, so a failure names the file you are in rather than a counter you have no way to move.
| 7 | **G-1 … G-5** (new) / **B-3** | **Partly closed by T30.** The groups exist: `Placement(anchor, spin, orient)` is a frozen, composable value wired into all 19 façade solid constructors, and giving it beside one of its own members raises the way a radius given beside its diameter does (G-3, D-5). Resolution took the opposite decision and it is recorded as G-4: `Facets` is **plumbing, not a public spelling**, because `use_defaults(fn=64)` already sets resolution for a block without threading anything through any call (R-4) and a group passed to every call would be strictly worse. What `Facets` does buy is G-5 — "an explicit value beats the ambient one" was implemented twice, once for the CSG facet controls and once for the SDF resolution, and both now go through `Facets.resolved()`. `Placement` now reads in two dimensions as well (G-1) and is wired into 8 of the 9 `flat.py` constructors: a placement carrying only an anchor and a spin serves a 2-D profile and the solid extruded from it alike, and one that sets a real `orient` **refuses** rather than quietly honouring two of its three members (G-6, E-5). The ninth is `text()`, whose `anchor` is a typographic baseline string rather than the anchor language — an O-6b defect of its own, recorded as item 7b. `EdgeTreatment` is built and wired into the 13 façade constructors that take both `rounding` and `chamfer`. The family turned out to be **two** groups, not the one the plan named: `rounding`+`chamfer` travels on 38 callables and `edges`+`except_edges` on 9, with only 5 taking all four — so a single four-member group would have lumped two families that mostly appear apart. What the group buys is G-7: rounding and chamfer are mutually exclusive, the library checked that in **six** places with six wordings and none of them said what to do instead, and one kind with one size leaves nothing to disagree. `EdgeSelection` (`edges` + `except_edges`, 15 callables) is built and wired into the two façade constructors that take the pair; unlike a treatment its members compose rather than conflict, so G-7 does not apply to it. **`Texturing` was not built, and the reason is item 7c:** its five parameters are advertised on 13 public constructors and every one of them refuses. The per-end variants (`rounding1`, `chamfer_angle`, …) that sit beside `EdgeTreatment` on ten constructors are B-3's duplication and were addressed by T31 from the other end: **67 façade defaults were `None` where a backend had a real value**, so the backend's default decided anything the caller left out and the two could resolve the same call differently. They are the façade's now, and `test_the_facade_owns_every_shared_default` keeps them there. Twenty-four remain `None` for a reason, in two groups: `res` (an ambient control — nothing to inherit means the backend's facet default is the answer, R-7) and `anchor` on the cylinders (the right value depends on `center`, so the backend computes it). The façade's parameter duplication (B-3) is untouched — a group removes three parameters from a signature that has forty. |
| 7a | **PLAN D-P4 / DOC-2** | **Partly closed by T35.** D-P4 has asked for a complete `Args:` on every public callable since it was written and nothing had ever checked: **313 public callables taking 1307 parameters documented none of them.** The 57 blocking the ambient-resolution work are written, so `tests/test_ambient_docs.py::KNOWN_GAPS` is empty and all 498 facet parameters now say where their default comes from. The remaining **256 across 38 files** are a per-file budget in `tests/test_documented_arguments.py` that only shrinks. A second check, unratcheted because it has always held, catches the different defect of a *partial* section — it found two, and both were real: `sdf.regular_prism` documented 8 of its parameters not at all, and `keyhole` declared an unused `_length` that a leading underscore now excludes. **How the 57 were written matters for the other 256:** harvesting "the most common wording for this parameter name" is not safe — it put a polyhedron's insphere radius on `cylindrical_extrude` and a cube-truss size on its `size`. What is safe is the *same-named* function's own wording (the SDF backend mirrors the CSG API, PAR-1) and the function a wrapper delegates to; those covered 416 of 586, and the remaining 170 were written by hand after reading each one. |
| 7b | **PLAN O-6b** | **Closed by T36.** `flat.text()` declared `anchor: str = "baseline"` while the other eight 2-D constructors take the anchor language, and it was the one `placement=` could not be wired into. It was never an anchor: the body read `valign if valign is not None else anchor`, so it was a **second spelling of `valign`** with a different default — a parallel vocabulary that also duplicated a parameter sitting beside it. `valign` owns the baseline default now and `anchor` is `Anchor | Sequence[float] | None`, applied to the finished text's box after the typographic alignment has placed it. `None` keeps that typographic placement, which is the usual answer for text and what every existing call gets. All nine 2-D constructors now take `placement=`.
| 7c | **G-8** (new) / **E-1 / E-2 / S-34 / S-35** | **Closed by T37 for `texture=`, the substantial one.** Four public capabilities were advertised and unbuilt, each refusing in a way `except Bosl2Error` could not catch; all four now raise `Bosl2NotImplementedError`, and **`texture=` is built**. S-34 and S-35 specify textures as a working subsystem and only the registry was: `cyl(texture=...)` refused on all five parameters. The cylinder family applies them now — the side is sampled on a grid of one column per texture cell, each vertex displaced radially, and both kinds of texture work because a VNF tile is rasterised to a height field first, which is what S-34's "the caller does not need to know which" asks for. The facet controls raise the column count so a coarse texture does not make a coarse cylinder (R-1), and `Texturing` (G-1) landed with it — the cleanest group in the library by G-1's own measure, and the last to be built because until now every one of its five parameters refused. The other three gaps remain, ratcheted in `tests/test_unimplemented.py`. |
| 8 | **C-23** (new) / **C-20** | **Closed by T33.** C-20 made the contract cover the whole object and said nothing about the cover meaning anything: **48 of the 90 members were declared `(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any)`** — found by name, checked not at all, so a caller following this project's own typing advice got every argument accepted including the wrong ones. Both families were loose for the same reason in the end — nobody had written the signatures out. The distribution family was obvious once looked at: all four implementations inherit one `Distributable` mixin and agree exactly. The attachment family *looked* like a harder case, because the SDF backend refuses it with a `(*_args: Any, **_kwargs: Any)` stub (PAR-3) and a loose implementation seems to force a loose contract. It does not: that form satisfies any protocol signature, so the contract was always free to declare the real one. 63 of 90 typed, and `base.attach("top", boss)` — C-20's own worked example, with the anchor mistyped — is a checker error instead of a silent pass. The remaining 27 are PLAN T-6c's genuine case, on a list that only shrinks.
| 9 | **PAR-3 / B-5 / PLAN B-P4** | **Closed by T34.** `fill` was in `CSG_ONLY_FEATURES` while `PyShape2D.fill()` worked anyway — extruding the field to a thin solid, meshing it, crossing to CSG, projecting to drop the holes and rebuilding an SDF polygon. That is B-5's silent lossy conversion and B-P4's third case, "listed as exclusive and *works anyway*, so the refusal never fires", exactly as `projection` behaved until T4. It refuses now, naming `.to_csg()` — the same round trip, said out loud. **The general finding was worth more than the fix:** the parity test walked `SdfSolid` and never `PyShape2D`, and `fill` is a 2-D operation, so nothing was ever going to catch it there. It walks both now, and a negative control confirms it fails when a listed feature quietly works.

## 13. Change process
1. A change altering a public signature MUST cite the requirement it serves in the commit body
   (`feat(solid): ambient resolution defaults — R-4`).
2. Adding a required parameter to an existing public callable is a breaking change and needs a
   default or a deprecation path.
3. Adding a façade shape follows B-7 and the parity rules in §7.1.
4. This document is updated in the same commit as any change to §4 (layering), §6 (subsystems),
   §7 (backends), or §8 (defaults). Language-level rules change in [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) instead.
5. **Requirement IDs are permanent.** Numbers are never reused or renumbered: a new requirement
   appends to its series, and a withdrawn one is struck through with the reason. Section numbers
   may move; IDs are what commits, tests and reviews cite.
